difficultyReason: Five conditional answer choices with reversed-conditional and scope-shift traps. The stimulus requires identifying that a person who acts on incomplete data cannot be held negligent — a subtle conceptual link buried in medical terminology.
stimulus: A physician who prescribes a medication without disclosing all known side effects to the patient is acting negligently. Dr. Chen prescribed a newly approved antiviral medication to a patient without disclosing several side effects that had appeared only in post-market surveillance reports published after the drug's approval. Some colleagues have argued that Dr. Chen acted negligently. This conclusion is unwarranted.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No physician can be expected to monitor post-market surveillance reports for every drug they prescribe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A physician does not act negligently unless the side effects that were not disclosed were known to the physician at the time of the prescription.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Post-market surveillance reports are less reliable than data gathered during clinical trials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any physician who discloses all side effects known at the time of prescription cannot be found negligent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physicians who prescribe newly approved medications are generally held to a lower standard of disclosure than those who prescribe established drugs.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes Dr. Chen was not negligent. The only premise available is that the side effects appeared in post-market reports published after approval — implying Dr. Chen did not know them at time of prescription. Choice B supplies the conditional: not negligent unless side effects were known at time of prescription. With B, the chain is complete: the side effects were not known to Dr. Chen at the time → Dr. Chen does not meet the condition for negligence → conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: This weakens the expectation on physicians generally but does not close the logical gap between 'unknown side effects' and 'not negligent.' It introduces a frequency qualifier ('every drug') that doesn't force the conclusion.
explanations.C: Reliability of the reports is irrelevant — the issue is whether Dr. Chen knew the side effects, not the quality of the data source.
explanations.D: This is the reversed conditional trap. The stimulus's negligence standard is 'fails to disclose known side effects → negligent'; choice D affirms the contrapositive of a different, weaker claim and does not force the conclusion about Dr. Chen.
explanations.E: This introduces a comparative standard not mentioned in the stimulus and at best makes the conclusion more plausible rather than logically necessitated.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a chain of economic terms with a scope shift between 'price-competitive' and 'profitable.' Reversed-conditional trap is prominent in choice D, and a too-weak trap appears in choice A.
stimulus: An industry analyst argues that any domestic manufacturer that cannot compete on price with foreign rivals will eventually lose its market share entirely. Helios Manufacturing has introduced a new automated production line that reduces its per-unit cost below that of its primary foreign competitor. The analyst's prediction, as applied to Helios, is therefore mistaken.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most domestic manufacturers that reduce their per-unit costs are able to compete on price with foreign rivals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any domestic manufacturer whose per-unit cost falls below that of its primary foreign competitor can compete on price with that competitor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helios Manufacturing's automated production line will not require costly maintenance that offsets its per-unit savings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any domestic manufacturer that retains its market share is one that can compete on price with foreign rivals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Automated production lines are the most effective means by which domestic manufacturers can achieve price competitiveness.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that the analyst's prediction does not apply to Helios. The prediction says: cannot compete on price → loses market share. To refute this for Helios, we need to show Helios CAN compete on price. The stimulus only tells us Helios's per-unit cost fell below its competitor's. Choice B supplies the missing link: per-unit cost below competitor's → can compete on price. This forces: Helios can compete on price → analyst's prediction does not apply → conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Too weak — 'most' does not guarantee that Helios is among those that can compete. A sufficient assumption needs universal or unambiguous coverage of the specific case.
explanations.C: This addresses a future contingency and at best makes the cost reduction more durable; it does not logically bridge per-unit cost to price competitiveness.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The analyst's claim is 'cannot compete → loses share'; the contrapositive is 'retains share → can compete.' Choice D states exactly this contrapositive but does nothing to establish that Helios retains its share or can compete — it merely restates a conditional that goes in the wrong direction for the argument.
explanations.E: Automation being the 'most effective' means is a comparative claim that does not force the conclusion about Helios specifically competing on price.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves an ethics argument about culpability with a subtle scope shift between 'foreseeable' and 'intended.' Five choices include a reversed conditional, a too-weak 'tends to' trap, and a principle-wrapping trap.
stimulus: Under our legal tradition, a person is morally culpable for an outcome only if that person either intended the outcome or could reasonably have foreseen it. Corporate executives at Vantara Inc. restructured employee pension plans in a way that eliminated retirement benefits for workers hired before 1990. The executives claim they did not intend this result. Several ethicists have argued that the executives are nonetheless morally culpable. Those ethicists are correct.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any restructuring of pension plans by corporate executives tends to produce outcomes that affect pre-1990 employees disproportionately.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corporate executives who restructure pension plans without consulting affected employees often fail to foresee the consequences of their actions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any corporate executive who restructures an employee pension plan could reasonably foresee how that restructuring would affect workers' benefits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A person is morally culpable for an outcome only if a reasonable person in that position would have intended the same outcome.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The elimination of retirement benefits for a class of workers is a more serious moral harm than any financial benefit the corporation might gain.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that the executives are morally culpable. They deny intent, but culpability requires either intent OR reasonable foreseeability. Choice C supplies the missing link: any corporate executive who restructures a pension plan could reasonably foresee the effects on benefits. With C, the executives satisfy the foreseeability prong → they are morally culpable → conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Too weak — 'tends to' does not establish that the executives specifically could reasonably foresee the outcome, which is what the culpability standard requires.
explanations.B: 'Often fail to foresee' cuts against culpability rather than supporting it, and 'often' is too weak regardless.
explanations.D: This is a scope-shift and reversal trap: it substitutes 'intended' for 'would have intended' and eliminates the foreseeability prong entirely, which actually makes the culpability standard harder to meet rather than supplying the missing link.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. The severity of the harm is irrelevant to the logical gap; the argument needs a link between the executives' actions and the conditions for culpability, not a moral ranking of outcomes.

difficultyReason: Environmental science domain with a multi-step conditional chain. The scope shift is between 'releases carbon' and 'accelerates warming.' Partial-bridge and reversed-conditional traps are both present.
stimulus: Any land-use practice that accelerates global warming should be prohibited by international treaty. Extensive research has established that draining coastal wetlands releases large quantities of carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere. Environmental advocates have therefore concluded that wetland drainage should be prohibited by international treaty.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any practice that should be prohibited by international treaty is one that releases large quantities of greenhouse gases.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No land-use practice that fails to release greenhouse gases accelerates global warming.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any land-use practice that releases large quantities of carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere accelerates global warming.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Draining coastal wetlands is among the land-use practices most frequently subject to international environmental agreements.

choices.label: E
choices.text: International treaties are the most effective mechanism for curtailing land-use practices that harm the environment.

explanations.correct: The argument needs two links: (1) releases large quantities of CO₂ and methane → accelerates global warming, and (2) accelerates global warming → should be prohibited. Link (2) is given in the stimulus. Choice C supplies link (1), completing the chain: wetland drainage releases large quantities of CO₂ and methane (given) → accelerates global warming (C) → should be prohibited by international treaty (given premise) → conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional trap. The given premise runs 'accelerates warming → should be prohibited.' Choice A states 'should be prohibited → releases greenhouse gases' — the reverse — which does not close the gap from 'releases gases' to 'should be prohibited.'
explanations.B: This addresses a negative condition (no gases → no warming) that is irrelevant; we already know wetland drainage does release gases, so this adds nothing to the chain.
explanations.D: Frequency of treaty coverage is irrelevant to whether wetland drainage should be prohibited; this is a partial-bridge trap.
explanations.E: A comparative claim about treaty effectiveness does not bridge the logical gap between releasing greenhouse gases and being prohibited.

difficultyReason: Technology domain with a scope shift between 'open-source' and 'publicly auditable.' Trap choices include a plausible but too-weak probabilistic answer and a reversed conditional. Students must identify the precise missing conditional link.
stimulus: Any encryption algorithm that is not publicly auditable cannot be trusted to protect sensitive government communications. The encryption algorithm embedded in the Argos secure messaging platform is proprietary and its source code has never been released to independent researchers. Therefore, the Argos platform should not be used for sensitive government communications.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most proprietary encryption algorithms contain vulnerabilities that have been exploited by adversarial state actors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any encryption algorithm whose source code has never been released to independent researchers is not publicly auditable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any encryption platform that should not be used for sensitive government communications is one whose source code has never been released.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No encryption algorithm that has been released to independent researchers can be trusted to protect sensitive government communications.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proprietary encryption algorithms are less likely than open-source algorithms to be subjected to independent security audits.

explanations.correct: The argument needs to connect 'source code never released to independent researchers' to 'not publicly auditable.' The given premise states: not publicly auditable → cannot be trusted → should not be used. Choice B supplies: source code never released → not publicly auditable. Combined with the premises, the chain is complete and the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Too weak — 'most' does not cover Argos specifically, and exploited vulnerabilities are not the same as being untrustworthy in the precise sense the argument requires.
explanations.C: Reversed conditional trap. The argument concludes 'should not be used → ···'; choice C states the reverse: 'should not be used → source code never released,' which tells us nothing about whether Argos falls into the prohibited category.
explanations.D: This is a scope-shift trap that addresses released algorithms, which are not the subject of the argument's conclusion about Argos.
explanations.E: Too weak — 'less likely' is probabilistic and cannot force a conclusion; it also shifts from 'not publicly auditable' to 'less likely to be audited.'

difficultyReason: Law domain. The stimulus involves a statutory interpretation argument with a scope shift between 'willful' and 'knowing.' The reversed-conditional trap is embedded in choice A, and choice E wraps a principle that sounds strong but uses different vocabulary.
stimulus: Under the Caldwell Act, a contractor is liable for damages only if the contractor willfully violated the terms of the contract. Pemberton Construction knowingly used substandard materials on the Harlow Bridge project, in direct contravention of the project's specifications. A trial court has ruled that Pemberton is liable for damages under the Caldwell Act. That ruling is correct.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any contractor who is liable for damages under the Caldwell Act is one who knowingly violated the terms of the contract.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any contractor who knowingly uses materials that contravene project specifications has willfully violated the terms of the contract.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No contractor who complies with project specifications can be found liable for damages under the Caldwell Act.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Caldwell Act was intended by its drafters to apply to contractors who use materials that endanger public safety.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contractors who repeatedly violate project specifications should be held to a higher standard of willfulness than first-time offenders.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that Pemberton is liable under the Caldwell Act. Liability requires willful violation (given). Pemberton is established to have knowingly used substandard materials. The gap is between 'knowingly' and 'willfully.' Choice B bridges this: knowingly using noncompliant materials = willfully violating the contract. With B, the chain is complete: Pemberton knowingly used substandard materials → Pemberton willfully violated the contract → Pemberton is liable → ruling is correct.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional trap. The Caldwell Act states 'willfully violated → liable'; choice A states 'liable → knowingly violated,' which is the reverse. This doesn't establish that Pemberton's knowing conduct satisfies the willfulness requirement.
explanations.C: This addresses compliance (the negative case) and does not help establish liability for Pemberton, who already violated specifications.
explanations.D: Legislative intent is a tool of interpretation, not a logical bridge between 'knowingly' and 'willfully'; it introduces new subject matter (public safety) absent from the argument.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. A comparative standard for repeated offenders is irrelevant to whether Pemberton's single instance of knowing noncompliance constitutes willfulness.

difficultyReason: Linguistics domain. The argument involves a scope shift between 'borrowed lexical items' and 'linguistic borrowing sufficient to alter syntactic structure.' Five conditional choices with partial-bridge and reversed traps.
stimulus: Linguists generally agree that a language undergoes structural change only when sustained contact with another language alters its syntactic patterns, not merely its vocabulary. Several scholars have argued that Medieval English underwent structural change due to contact with Norman French. Their argument relies entirely on evidence that Norman French contributed thousands of lexical borrowings to English. This evidence does not support the scholars' conclusion.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No language that borrows vocabulary from another language ever undergoes structural change as a result of that contact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medieval English adopted more lexical borrowings from Latin than from Norman French.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lexical borrowing alone, without accompanying changes to syntactic patterns, does not constitute the kind of sustained contact that produces structural change in a language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any language that undergoes structural change as a result of contact with another language must also borrow lexical items from that language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The syntactic patterns of Medieval English were more resistant to external influence than those of contemporary English.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that lexical borrowing evidence doesn't support the claim of structural change. The given principle is: structural change requires sustained contact that alters syntactic patterns (not merely vocabulary). Choice C makes explicit that lexical borrowing alone does not constitute the required contact. This forces the conclusion: the scholars' evidence (lexical borrowings) → does not demonstrate altered syntactic patterns → does not show the requisite sustained contact → does not support the structural change conclusion.
explanations.A: Too strong and introduces a different claim. The argument doesn't require that vocabulary borrowing never co-occurs with structural change — it only needs to show that lexical evidence alone doesn't prove structural change. Choice A overclaims and would be empirically problematic.
explanations.B: A comparative claim about Latin vs. French borrowings is irrelevant to the logical gap between lexical evidence and structural-change conclusions.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The principle implies 'structural change → sustained syntactic contact'; choice D states 'structural change → lexical borrowing,' which is a different and weaker claim that does not address the sufficiency of lexical evidence.
explanations.E: Resistance of syntactic patterns is a historical claim that, even if true, does not logically connect the lexical evidence to the insufficiency of the scholars' conclusion.

difficultyReason: History domain. Multi-conditional chain with scope shift between 'military campaign' and 'politically motivated.' Reversed conditional is in choice D; too-weak trap in choice A; principle-wrapping trap in choice E.
stimulus: Historical actions taken solely to consolidate a ruler's domestic political power are not genuine military campaigns; they are political theater. Contemporary chronicles record that Emperor Aldric III launched his invasion of the Varell provinces primarily to suppress dissent among his noble rivals at court. Critics who describe the Varell invasion as one of the great military campaigns of the medieval period are therefore mistaken.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most military historians distinguish between invasions motivated by territorial ambition and those motivated by domestic political considerations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any invasion launched primarily to suppress domestic political dissent is an action taken solely to consolidate a ruler's domestic political power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Emperor Aldric III had no genuine territorial or strategic ambitions in the Varell provinces at the time of the invasion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any action that constitutes political theater rather than a genuine military campaign was launched primarily to suppress domestic dissent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The greatness of a military campaign should be assessed by its strategic consequences rather than by the scale of forces involved.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that describing the Varell invasion as a genuine military campaign is mistaken. The given principle: actions taken solely to consolidate domestic political power → not genuine military campaigns. The chronicles establish: Aldric launched the invasion primarily to suppress dissent among noble rivals. The gap is between 'primarily to suppress court dissent' and 'solely to consolidate domestic political power.' Choice B closes that gap: any invasion launched primarily to suppress domestic political dissent = action taken solely to consolidate domestic political power. The chain is complete and the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Too weak — 'most historians' and their distinctions are neither universal nor directly applicable to the Varell invasion; this does not force the conclusion.
explanations.C: Even if Aldric had no territorial ambitions, this does not by itself establish that the invasion falls under the 'solely to consolidate political power' category without the bridge choice B provides. It is a partial bridge at best.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The given principle runs: solely political → not genuine campaign. Choice D states: political theater → launched primarily to suppress dissent, which is the reverse direction and adds nothing to the argument.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. Assessment criteria for greatness are irrelevant to the logical question of whether the invasion was a genuine military campaign at all.

difficultyReason: Policy domain with a subtle scope shift between 'publicly funded' and 'subject to open-records requirements.' Five conditional choices with a reversed conditional, a too-weak probabilistic answer, and a partial-bridge trap.
stimulus: Any institution that is subject to open-records requirements must disclose all communications pertaining to the use of public funds. The Dellwood Foundation accepted a substantial grant from the state government to fund its community health programs and has refused to disclose internal communications about how the grant money was allocated. Critics argue that Dellwood has violated open-records requirements. Their argument is well-founded.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Private foundations that accept state grants are more likely to misuse public funds than government agencies that administer those funds directly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any institution that discloses all communications about public fund use has complied with open-records requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any private foundation that accepts a state government grant thereby becomes subject to open-records requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any institution that violates open-records requirements is one that has accepted public funding from a government source.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Open-records requirements were designed primarily to ensure that institutions managing public funds remain accountable to taxpayers.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that Dellwood violated open-records requirements. The given rule is: subject to open-records requirements → must disclose all communications about public funds. Dellwood accepted a state grant and refused to disclose. The gap is between 'accepted a state grant' and 'subject to open-records requirements.' Choice C supplies this exactly: any private foundation accepting a state grant → subject to open-records requirements. With C, the chain is: Dellwood accepted a state grant → subject to open-records requirements → must disclose → refused to disclose → violated requirements. The conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Too weak and probabilistic — 'more likely to misuse' does not establish that Dellwood is subject to open-records requirements or that it violated them.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The given rule runs: subject to requirements → must disclose. Choice B states: discloses → complied, which is the compliant case and does nothing to establish that Dellwood, which refused to disclose, violated the requirements without first establishing Dellwood was subject to them.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. This states: violated open-records → accepted public funding. This is the converse of what is needed and does not help establish that Dellwood was subject to the requirements.
explanations.E: Legislative purpose is irrelevant to the logical gap; even if true, it does not close the chain between accepting a state grant and being subject to the requirements.

difficultyReason: Arts domain mirroring the Peacock/Hacker paradigm: a critic's claim is refuted by a counterexample, and the correct answer must establish that the counterexample's property is incompatible with the critic's characterization. Reversed-conditional and principle-wrapping traps are prominent.
stimulus: Several critics have asserted that any composer who relies exclusively on algorithmic procedures to generate musical material is incapable of genuine artistic expression. This claim is without merit. Consider Lena Voss and Dario Ferrante, two celebrated composers whose work is generated entirely through algorithmic processes and who are widely recognized in the concert world as artists of remarkable expressive depth and originality.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No composer who is widely recognized as an artist of expressive depth relies exclusively on algorithmic procedures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any composer who is widely recognized as an artist of remarkable expressive depth and originality is capable of genuine artistic expression.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Algorithmic procedures can generate musical structures that are indistinguishable from those produced by non-algorithmic composition methods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any composer who is capable of genuine artistic expression will eventually abandon exclusive reliance on algorithmic procedures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The originality of a musical work is determined primarily by the composer's conceptual intent rather than by the method used to generate its material.

explanations.correct: The argument refutes the critics by pointing to Voss and Ferrante as composers who use exclusively algorithmic procedures yet possess 'remarkable expressive depth and originality.' For this counterexample to defeat the claim that algorithmic composers are incapable of genuine artistic expression, we need: recognized expressive depth → capable of genuine artistic expression. Choice B supplies exactly this. Combined with the premise that Voss and Ferrante are recognized as artists of remarkable expressive depth, the chain is: Voss and Ferrante are recognized as having expressive depth and originality (given) → they are capable of genuine artistic expression (B) → the critics' claim that algorithmic composers are incapable is false → conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional and subject-shift trap. Choice A states: widely recognized expressive depth → not exclusively algorithmic. This directly contradicts the premises about Voss and Ferrante and would actually undermine the argument, not support it.
explanations.C: This addresses the output of algorithmic processes, not whether the composer is capable of genuine artistic expression — a scope shift that does not close the logical gap.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. Choice D implies capable of expression → eventually abandons algorithms, which is irrelevant to and inconsistent with the counterexample's force.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap, echoing Peacock choice (E). Even if conceptual intent is the primary determinant of originality, this does not entail that recognized expressive depth constitutes capability of genuine artistic expression — the precise link the argument requires.
